`c1ccc2c(c1)C(C)(C)C(O)C2(C)C` -> Naphthalene core reduced on one ring.
Positions: 1,2,3,4-tetrahydronaphthalene.
At position 2: OH and methyl? No, `C(C)(C)C(O)C2(C)C` means at the bridgehead carbon (position 1), there are two methyls `C(C)(C)`. At position 2, there is an OH `C(O)`. At position 3, there is a methyl `C2(C)C`? Wait, `C2(C)C` closes the ring at position 4? Let's parse SMILES: `c1ccc2c(c1)C(C)(C)C(O)C2(C)C`
Ring 1: c1ccc2c(c1) -> benzene fused to a 6-membered ring.
The saturated ring atoms: C(C)(C) - this is a quaternary carbon with two methyls. Then C(O) - tertiary alcohol. Then C2(C)C - wait, this closes back to the second ring atom? Actually, `C2` closes the ring. So the saturated ring has 4 carbons: C(quat), C(OH), C(Me), and the other bridgehead.
So it's a 1,1,3-trimethyl-2-hydroxy-1,2,3,4-tetrahydronaphthalene derivative? Or maybe 1,1,3,3-tetramethyl? Let's count: `C(C)(C)` is C1 with two Me. `C(O)` is C2 with OH. `C2(C)C` is C3 with one Me? Wait, `C2` indicates closure to atom labeled '2'. In `c1ccc2`, '2' is the first saturated carbon. So `C2(C)C` means the atom closing the ring has a methyl substituent. That would be C4 of the tetralin. So it's 1,1,3,4-tetramethyl-2-hydroxy-1,2,3,4-tetrahydronaphthalene? Or maybe just 1,1,3-trimethyl.
